questions.title: Audio-dependent listener behavior
questions.comment: I note that the authors have clearly stated the limitations of ∆Resp in the appendix. Existing human preference, MLLM behavior detection, and motion evaluations support that the generated results exhibit more visible listener behaviors and higher naturalness, but they are not yet sufficient to distinguish whether these behaviors undergo meaningful temporal changes in response to another speaker's audio track, or mainly stem from a conversational scene motion prior that does not depend on the other party's audio track.
questions.intro: Compare each audio pair. The image, other audio track, and generic prompt are fixed.

questions.title: Multi-person component ablations
questions.comment: The architectural ablations in Table 4 are conducted solely under the single-person HDTF setting using the Stage-1 1.3B model. While these ablations support the contribution of relevant components to single-person generation quality, they have not directly verified the respective effects of reference face features and spatial region constraints on multi-person audio binding, listener behaviors, and person-count extrapolation, which limits the explanation of the mechanism behind the performance gains.
questions.intro: Compare component variants across two, three, and four people.

questions.title: Data scale and uncertainty
questions.comment: Table 3 has supported the effectiveness of concatenated pre-training under the same 1.3B model scale, but performance variation curves across different real two-person data scales under a fixed training budget have not yet been reported; therefore, existing results can support that the strategy is effective under the 12-hour real data setting, but are still insufficient to fully characterize how its real-data efficiency varies with data scale, and it is also difficult to quantify the extent of real data saved solely through cross-system comparisons with MultiTalk. Regarding person-count extrapolation, the three-person and four-person tests each contain only 20 videos, and confidence intervals are not reported for the main results.
questions.intro: E7: fixed-update data scaling. E8: unique-data learning curves. E9: difference confidence intervals.

questions.title: Audio interventions
questions.comment: Under the premise of fixing the reference image, the listener's own audio track, and the random seed, if interventions are applied only to the other speaker's audio track (such as temporal shifting, altering pause/turn-taking rhythms, or muting? ), will the generated listener actions (nodding, head-turning, or gaze events) exhibit interpretable temporal changes accordingly?
questions.intro: Compare each audio pair. The image, other audio track, and generic prompt are fixed.

questions.title: Component ablations
questions.comment: If the architectural ablation variants already defined in Table 4 are directly extended to the two person as well as three and four person test sets of InteractivePerson, what are the performance differences among the components in multi person lip binding, listener reaction metrics, and person-count extrapolation?
questions.intro: Compare component variants across two, three, and four people.

questions.title: Difference confidence intervals
questions.comment: Please additionally provide the confidence intervals on the main objective metrics and human preferences for the InteractivePerson test set.
questions.intro: Metric and preference differences with 95% confidence intervals for two to four people.

questions.title: Real-data scaling
questions.comment: As a suggestion to more fully characterize the boundaries of the method, providing performance trends across different real two person data scales under a fixed 1.3B model and training budget, or offering a stratified quantitative analysis regarding the degree of substantial subject deviation from the first-frame fixed mask and regional overlap, would help more accurately define the data efficiency and scope of applicability.
questions.intro: E7 varies dataset size at 5,000 updates. E8 tracks cumulative unique training hours.

questions.title: Audio and text controls
questions.comment: Figure 4 checks whether reactions occur, but not whether they happen at the right time or match what the speaker says. The responsiveness metric measures average movement during listening, and human preferences measure overall naturalness. Neither establishes that reactions depend on the speaker’s audio. The model also accepts text, but only generic prompts are tested. It therefore remains unclear whether the listener movements are meaningful responses or general listening behaviors.
questions.intro: Use E1–E4 for audio changes and E14/E15 for text instructions.

questions.title: Ablations and data scaling
questions.comment: Table 4 tests the architectural components only on single-person videos using the smaller model. This does not show how these components prevent one person from following another person’s audio or support generation with more people. Table 3 tests training data choices with two people, but not larger groups. The data-efficiency claim also needs comparisons using different amounts of real conversation data under the same training budget.
questions.intro: E5/E6: component and data ablations. E7/E8: data-scaling comparisons.

questions.title: Audio interventions
questions.comment: If one speaker’s audio is changed while the listener’s audio, reference image, prompt, and random seed remain fixed, do the listener’s reactions change appropriately? Please evaluate reaction timing and relevance, rather than occurrence alone.
questions.intro: Compare each audio pair. The image, other audio track, and generic prompt are fixed.

questions.title: Text control
questions.comment: Can text prompts control a specific listener’s gaze, nods, or other reactions? Please show matched examples that vary only the instruction, or clarify that explicit reaction control is outside the method’s scope.
questions.intro: Each case compares the generic prompt with one gaze instruction. Image, audio, seed, and sampling are fixed.

questions.title: Component and data ablations
questions.comment: Can the architectural and data ablations be evaluated on three, and four person inputs, including incorrect mouth activation during silence and responses to another person’s audio?
questions.intro: E5/E6 compare component and data variants; E3/E1 show audio interventions.

questions.title: Listener gaze
questions.comment: The three- and four-person results show visible listener movements, but do not establish whether each listener responds to the appropriate speaker. In larger groups, who determines which participant a speaker addresses and which listeners should react? Please assess directed gaze and listener responses around speaker changes, rather than only whether reactions occur somewhere in the video.
questions.intro: Compare generated clips with ground truth over the same interval. E13 includes a speaker change.

questions.title: Real-data scaling
questions.comment: How does performance change with different amounts of real-conversation refinement data under matched training budgets? Does concatenated pretraining consistently reduce the amount needed?
questions.intro: E7 varies dataset size at 5,000 updates. E8 tracks cumulative unique training hours.

questions.title: Training-data efficiency
questions.comment: The overall approach feels like an engineering-level trick, as opposed to a principled new technique that has a novel breakthrough.  The two-stage training makes sense overall.  However, I'd like to challenge that the two-person or multiple-person videos are also widely available, based on previous method, despite it requires annoation. Can the authors provide more specific unit economic numbers to justify that training on 2000 hours of video data is better than asking people to do the annotation?  Also, the multiple-person interactions from real videos are more nuanced than any synthetic dataset, would a smaller set of real data but with rich annoation would beat the proposed methodology from both economic and performance perspective? The authors should provide this discussion.
questions.intro: Use E6 for training-data ablations and E7/E8 for real-data scaling.

questions.title: Metric and human agreement
questions.comment: The proposed method quantifies listener motion, but its validity as a measure of natural interactivity is not sufficiently established. I personally feel the resulting video is very unnatural (i.e., gaze directions & facial expressions). This metric should be validated against blinded human ratings.
questions.intro: E10 reports agreement with human preferences; E12/E13 and E1 provide video examples.

questions.title: Pretraining and refinement
questions.comment: Besides, I don't see any deep, insightful analysis of why the first-stage training would "ease" the second-stage training.
questions.intro: Use E6 for training-data ablations and E7/E8 for real-data scaling.

questions.title: Training-data scale
questions.comment: Do you see any scaling law applies in either the first stage or the second stage training? Why 2000 hours, why not 200 hours or 20000 hours, how does that curve look like for the final performance.
questions.intro: E7/E8 compare stage-2 real-data scaling from two pretraining initializations.
